questions.explanation: `b` is scheduled when it is created, but `a` is lazy and does not start until `a.await()`. At that point `a` is queued behind `b`, and the main coroutine suspends. The event loop runs `b` first, then `a`, and finally resumes the sum. A lazy `async` that nobody starts would never run.

questions.question: Which statement about marking a function `suspend` is true?
options: It makes the function run on `Dispatchers.IO` unless another dispatcher is given
It lets the function suspend; it does not move work to a background thread by itself
It makes blocking calls inside the function, like `Thread.sleep`, non-blocking
It makes the function start a new coroutine on the caller's scope each time it is called
questions.explanation: `suspend` only means the function can pause and resume later, and that it must be called from a coroutine or another suspend function. It runs on whatever dispatcher the caller is using. Blocking calls inside it still block the thread; you need `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` or a suspending API to avoid that.

questions.question: Why should parsing a large JSON payload use `Dispatchers.Default` rather than `Dispatchers.IO`?
options: Dispatchers.IO cannot run suspend functions, only plain blocking Java calls
Parsing is CPU-bound; Default has about one thread per core, which suits CPU work
Dispatchers.IO is single-threaded, so parsing there would block all other network calls
Dispatchers.Default runs on the main thread, so the parsed result can update the UI directly
questions.explanation: Default is sized to the number of CPU cores, which is the right amount of parallelism for CPU work. IO allows many more threads (64 by default) because those threads mostly wait on blocking I/O; running CPU work there can create more busy threads than cores. Neither dispatcher is the main thread, and IO is not single-threaded.

questions.question: Switching from `Dispatchers.Default` to `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` often does not move the coroutine to a different thread, because the two dispatchers share one thread pool.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Dispatchers.IO and Dispatchers.Default share the same pool of threads and only have different limits on how many run at once. Switching between them often continues on the same thread with no real thread switch. The limits still apply, so the switch still matters for how much parallel work is allowed.

questions.question: Which statements about `launch` and `async` are true? Select all that apply.
options: `runBlocking` is the recommended way to call suspend functions from a ViewModel
`async` without `await` is the recommended way to fire and forget work
`launch` blocks the calling thread until its body finishes
`launch` returns a `Job`; `async` returns a `Deferred<T>`, which is also a `Job`
With the default start mode, both schedule their coroutine right away without waiting for `join` or `await`
questions.explanation: `Deferred` extends `Job` and adds `await()` for the result. Both builders start eagerly by default. `launch` does not block anything; it returns a Job right away. For fire-and-forget work use `launch`, since an unawaited `async` hides its result and can hide errors. `runBlocking` blocks the thread and belongs in `main` or tests, not in a ViewModel.

questions.question: Two coroutines are launched inside `runBlocking` on its single thread. Each one waits 1 second and then prints. About how long does it take if they use `Thread.sleep(1000)` versus `delay(1000)`?
options: About 2 seconds with both, because there is only one thread
About 2 seconds with Thread.sleep, about 1 second with delay
About 1 second with both, because coroutines always run in parallel
About 1 second with Thread.sleep, about 2 seconds with delay
questions.explanation: `Thread.sleep` blocks the only thread, so the second coroutine cannot start its wait until the first finishes. `delay` suspends and frees the thread, so both waits overlap. Coroutines are concurrent, not automatically parallel.

questions.question: On Android, what is the difference between `Dispatchers.Main` and `Dispatchers.Main.immediate`?
options: `immediate` cannot be cancelled, so code started with it always finishes even if the scope is cancelled
`immediate` makes `delay()` return at once, which is used to speed up UI tests
`immediate` uses a higher-priority thread than the main thread, so UI updates skip the frame queue
If already on the main thread, `immediate` runs the code at once instead of posting it to the queue
questions.explanation: `Dispatchers.Main` always posts the work to the main Handler, even if the caller is already on the main thread, which delays it by at least one queue turn. `Main.immediate` skips that post when it is already on the main thread. `viewModelScope` and `lifecycleScope` use it to avoid needless delays and flicker. It is still the same main thread and follows normal cancellation.

questions.question: How does the Kotlin compiler implement a `suspend` function on the JVM?
options: It keeps a copy of the whole call stack on the heap and restores it when the function resumes
It runs the body on a separate Java thread and blocks the caller with a lock until that thread finishes
It adds a `Continuation` parameter and compiles the body into a resumable state machine
It turns each suspend call into a callback passed to `Dispatchers.Default`, which then calls the rest of the body
questions.explanation: This is continuation-passing style: the caller passes a `Continuation`, and the body becomes a state machine that saves its locals in that object at each suspension point. When it suspends, it returns `COROUTINE_SUSPENDED`, and the thread is free. No extra thread is used and the whole stack is not copied, which is why coroutines are cheap.
